Surūpa and Surūpā, Guṇeśa, Gau, Kalakaṇṭha, Vṛkodara;

Immediately after the section on the forehead (*lalāṭaka*), this pentad of verses is seen in some places as an addition:
"The Half-Measure (*ardhamātrā*), the *Kalā*, the *Vāṇī*, the *Nāda*, the Crescent Moon (*ardhendu*), and Sadāśiva;
the *Anucāryā*, the Fourth (*turyā*), the Universal Mother (*viśvamātṛkalā*), and the Supreme (*parā*). [This is] the *Nāda*."
*Namaḥ* (salutation) means worship in the heart, ritual placement (*nyāsa*), bowing, bending, and prostration;

The syllable *a* is Vāsudeva, and the syllable *ā* is the Grandfather (Brahmā);
the syllable *ā* is also proclaimed to be used for worship and for auspiciousness.
The letter *i* is said to be desire (*kāma*), and the letter *ī* is said to be Lakṣmī;
the letter *u* is declared to be Śaṅkara, and the letter *ū* is for protection.
The letter *ṛ* is the mother of the gods; the letter *ṝ* is the progenitor of the Danujas.
The letter *ḷ* is the womb of the gods, and the letter *ḹ* is said by the wise to be the mother.
The letter *e* is said to be Viṣṇu, and the letter *ai* is Maheśvara;
the letter *o* shall be Brahmā, and the letter *au* is called Rudra. 4.
The syllable *aṃ* is the supreme Brahman; *aḥ* is the god Maheśvara;
*ka* is declared to be Prajāpati, and *ka* is said to be Vāyu. || 5 ||

What is declared to be the self (ātman), and what is cited as illumination (prakāśa)? What is declared to be the head (ka), and what is proclaimed as water (ka)? What is celebrated as happiness (sukha)? 12–6.
Svāhā, Parā, Devabhojyā, two Ṭhas, a pair of Candras;
The tuft (śikhā) is *vaṣaṭ*, the center of the head, the mother of Śakra, and the beloved of Hara. *Vaṣaṭ*.
The one called Krodha is HŪṂ; the armor is HŪṂ, and the weapons and missiles are designated as the enemy. HŪṂ.

With *phaṭ* for the weapons and missiles, there should be a snap of the fingers; at the end of the limbs, *su* denotes the gods. *Phaṭ*.
(p. 24) 1. On earth, *kuḥ* is well-known; *kuḥ* is also proclaimed in the sense of contempt.
The faculty of space has been fully explained; space is declared to be the ether (ākāśa). || 7 ||
The syllable *kham* is declared to mean heaven, and *kham* is proclaimed to mean a serpent;
likewise, they say *kham* refers to a chasm, and *kham* is proclaimed to mean emptiness.
Ga is declared to be Gaṇapati; Go is proclaimed as Gandharva.
Gaṃ is song (gīta), Gā is a verse (gāthā), Gau is a cow (dhenus), and Gau is Sarasvatī.
The cow is also designated as the mother; on earth, the cow is celebrated [as such]. 8. The letter *gha* is declared to be the bell; *ghā* is celebrated as the small bell (*kiṅkiṇī*). 10.
The sound *gha* is declared to be used for comparison; *ghu* is proclaimed for a bad sound. *Ghā* is declared for killing; *gha* is proclaimed for scenting. || 11 ||
The letter Ṅa is known as Bhairava; the letter Ṅa is remembered as the sense-object.
12 The letter Ca is known as the Moon; the letter Cha is proclaimed as the thief. 12.
The letter *cha* is declared to mean "pure," and it is proclaimed to mean "a boat";
the letter *cha* is also declared by learned scholars skilled in words to mean "cutting. (13)
The syllable *ja* is declared in the *vegita* (swift) meter, and *ja* is proclaimed in the *jaghana* (hip) meter;
furthermore, *ja* is declared as the *jetā* (conqueror) by those renowned as experts in prosody. 14–16.
The syllable *jha* occurs in a storm; *jha* is also declared when something has perished. The syllable *ña* is said to be in singing; *ña* is in a gurgling sound. (15)
Ṭa is proclaimed in the sound "ṭaṅkāra," ṭā on the earth, and ṭo in sound;
ṭha is proclaimed in the void, and ṭho is declared to be Maheśvara. || 16 ||
The syllable *ṭha* is said to be in the great sound and likewise in the orb of the moon;
the letter *ḍa* is said to be in Śaṅkara and is proclaimed to be in the sounds of terror. (17)
The letter *ḍha* is proclaimed as the *ḍhakkā* drum, and also in the sound that is devoid of qualities (*nirguṇa*).
The letter *ṇa* is proclaimed as knowledge (*jñāna*), and is also celebrated in the sense of ascertainment (*nirṇaya*). (18)
The letter *ta* is said to be a thief; it is proclaimed to be in the chest and the tail.
(4) The letter *tha* should be on the mountain of stone; the letter *tha* is for protection from fear. (19)
Da is declared to mean "wife"; do occurs in the senses of "giving," "cutting," and "elements";
dha is used for "wealth" and "the Lord of Wealth" (Kubera); and dho and dhā are shown to mean "the Creator. || 20 ||
*Dhiṣaṇā* is explained as *dhī* (intellect); *dhū* refers to both burden and anxiety.
|| 8 || The letter *na* is proclaimed [to signify] the Sugata and bondage; *nu* is celebrated in the sense of praise. || 21 ||
The letter *na* is declared to mean "leader" (*netṛ*) and "water" (*nī*); the word *nau* is proclaimed to mean "boat" (*taraṇi*).
The letter *na* is celebrated as signifying the "Well-Gone One" (*sugata*), "awakened one" (*buddha*), "praise" (*stuti*), and "sun" (*sūrya*). (22)
The word *na* is proclaimed for a welcome, a kinsman, a tree, and the sun;
(12) *pa* is well-known as Kubera and is also proclaimed in the west. (23)
The letter *pa* is declared to signify wind (*pavana*), while *pā* signifies drinking (*pāna*) and the drinker (*pātṛ*).
The letter *pha* occurs in the sense of phlegm (*kapha*) and wind (*vāta*), and is likewise proclaimed to signify calling (*āhvāna*). || 24 ||
The letter *pha* is proclaimed to represent a gale,
and the letter *phi* is likewise declared to signify anger as well as fruitless speech.
The syllable *ba* is said to be in the region of the chest and is also cited in relation to the mace;
the asterism is called *bha* by the wise, while *bha* is proclaimed to be in the bee. (26)
*Bhā* is said by the wise to mean radiance, *bhūḥ* means the earth, and *bhīḥ* means fear.
(20) *Maḥ* is proclaimed as Śiva, the Moon, and Brahmā; and *mā* is celebrated as Lakṣmī. (27)
The syllable *mū* is proclaimed to signify the mother, pride, and bondage;
while *yaḥ* is said by the learned to mean fame, or it is designated as the wind. (28)
That which is taught by those who know the terminology regarding the vehicle (*yāna*), the traveler (*yātṛ*), and renunciation (*tyāga*):
*ra* occurs in the sense of desire (*kāma*), wind (*anila*), fire (*vahni*), and sound (*śabda*); *ru* is likewise proclaimed [in these senses]. || 29 ||
Ra is proclaimed for wealth, ri for sovereignty, ru for grain, and ra for fear.
(4) La is for Indra and salt; lā is for giving and also for joining. (30)
The letter *la* signifies adhesion, the heart, dissolution, and also means accomplishment;
the letter *la* also signifies the mind, Varuṇa, and consolation. (31)
Pracetā is declared for you; Kalasa is proclaimed for you. (8) Pakṣī is designated for you; Viḥ is proclaimed for the act of going. (32)
The wise declare that *śam* is the highest good (*śreyas*), and the Teacher (*śāstṛ*) is also said to be *śam*.
They say that *śīḥ* is rest (*śasaṃ*) and lying down (*śayana*), while *śūḥ* is declared to be violence (*hiṃsā*). || 33 ||
The letter *ṣa* is proclaimed in the sense of "excellent," and *ṣū* in the sense of "delivering from the womb";
the letter *ṣa* is also fully proclaimed [to occur] after a prefix (*upasarga*) and in the sense of the remote past (*parokṣa*). 12, 34.
That is declared to be the prefix *apa-*, and she is called Lakṣmī;
that [prefix] occurs in the sense of "anger" (*kopa*) and "instrument" (*karaṇa*), and likewise it is proclaimed in relation to the Wielder of the Trident (*śūlin*). (35)
The letter *sa* is said to be the monkey; the letter *sa* is called "all.
That very [letter] is declared to be the cow, and that is proclaimed to be the union. 16, 36.
The syllable *haḥ* may signify anger or even maintenance; *haḥ* is proclaimed as [the seed-syllable of] Śūlinī.
The syllable *hiḥ* is said to be used for completing a verse; *hiḥ* may also be used for indicating a reason or for emphasis. (37)
The syllable *kṣa* is declared by those who know the science of words to signify "field," "protector," and "restrainer.
The syllable *kṣi* is proclaimed to mean "field," "the protection of the kṣatriyas," and "Nṛsiṃha."
Thus ends the Ekākṣarakoṣa composed by the illustrious Puruṣottamadeva.

A Vidyujjihvā, Ā Kālavajrī, I Garjinī, Ī Dhūmrabhairavī, U Kālarātri, Ū Vidārī, Ṛ Mahāraudrī, Ṝ Bhayaṅkarī, Ḷ Saṃhāriṇī, Ḹ Karālinī, E Ūrdhvakeśī, AI Ugrabhairavī, O Bhīmākṣī, AU Ḍākinī, AṂ Rudrarākiṇī, AḤ Caṇḍikā; KA Krodhīśa, KHA Vāmana, GA Caṇḍa, GHA Vikārī, ṄA Unmattabhairava, CA Jvālāmukha, CHA Raktadaṃṣṭra, JA Asitāṅga, JHA Baḍavāmukha, ÑA Vidyunmukha, ṬA Mahājvāla.

O beloved, the mouth of the Veda is certainly the seed of poison, like the Hālāhala venom.
Caṇḍīśa, mounted upon blood and adorned by Dhūmrabhairavī, joined with Nāda and Bindu, is considered the seed-syllable dear to Viṣṇu: Śrīṃ.
Residing in blood, with a face like the sky, adorned by Dhūmrabhairavī, and joined with Nāda and Bindu—this is remembered as the first seed-syllable (the variant reading for Māyā is "Lajjā"). Hrīṃ.
Krodhīśa, mounted upon blood and adorned by Dhūmrabhairavī, joined with Nāda and Bindu, is known as Pitṛbhūvāsinī; [the seed-syllable] is *krī*.

O Goddess worshipped by heroes, know that the *kūrca* mantra consists of *vidārī*, followed by *vyomāsya*, adorned with *rudra* and *rākiṇī*, and ending with *kāla* and the seed-syllable of *krodha*: *HŪM*.
Having taken up the fierce Bhairavī, who is joined with *nāda* and *bindu*, know, O beloved, that the seed-syllable *ai* is the elemental *vāgbhava*, the essence of Sarasvatī. 12.
O Dear One, the mantra of the weapon is known as the great-flamed fire of dissolution; *phaṭ*.
Krodhīśa is red with terrifying eyes; this is the goad (aṅkuśa) endowed with Nāda and Bindu: Kroṃ.
The head [mantra] is *dviṭhaḥ* (the letter ṭha with the vowel i), followed by the wife of fire (*vahni-jāyā*), which is *svāhā*; this is the beloved of the blazing one. *Svāhā*.
Krodhīśa, Balabhit, Dhūmra-bhairavī, Nāda, and Bindu; Trimūrti, Manmatha, Kāma—the seed-syllable that deludes the three worlds: *klīṃ*.

With the sky as its mouth, enriched by the Night of Time (Kālarātri), and the armor-syllable joined with the drop and the moon—this is declared to be the seed-mantra of the armor for you, O stainless one who delights in the Kula conduct. Hūṃ.
With the sky as its mouth, mounted upon blood, and with the *bindus* of the sound of the *ḍākinīs*, this mantra of light is proclaimed as the destroyer of great sins: *hrauṃ*.
Joined with Dhūmrabhairavī, residing in the syllable *rakta*, the consumer of offerings (*balibhojana*),
and endowed with *nāda* and *bindu*, this is the supreme seed-syllable of Kiṅkiṇī: *drīṃ*.
Having taken up the multiform one who stands drenched in blood, likewise having torn [the heart] and embraced it, the Great Mantra is for the sake of the specific goal. Bhrūṃ.
Beneath the smoke-bannered fire (Dhūmadhvaja) is Kālāgni, together with upward-pointing hair, the moon, and the bindu;
this seed-syllable that brings about the end of the age was revealed by Bhairava: *Sphreṃ*.
Saṃhāriṇī is based on [the letter] Ū, while Kapardinī is based on Ṛ;
the seed-syllable joined with Nāda and Bindu is known as Vaitālika. Pḷ-e&.
Taking the Bindu from the beginning and Krodhīśa situated in Saṃhāriṇī, it is called the seed-syllable of Kampinī; Manoharī is said to be preceded by Dviṭha. *Kliṛīṃ svāhā*.
Having taken up Kapardin, who stands smeared with blood, joined with Dhūmrabhairavī; this is the crow (KṢA), possessing the nasal sound (NĀDA) and the bindu (M). Prīṃ.
Taking up two skull-cups, it is adorned by Mahākāla; this is declared to be the excellent seat, enriched by Caṇḍikā and captivating to the mind. Ṭhaṭhaṃ ṭhaḥ ṭhaḥ.
Established in the fire of dissolution, bearing the banner of smoke, with the bindu in the secret place and joined with Dhūmrabhairavī—O Dear One, she is remembered as Phetkāriṇī. Sphīṃ.
Seated upon blood, with a face like the sky, adorned with a dot, a crescent moon, and the letter *la*, she is renowned as Khadyota; she is the devourer joined with Kālarātri. Hrūṃ.
The seed-syllable of the son of Vivasvat (Yama), "Hrūṃ," is situated in blood, has the sky as its mouth, is endowed with the *nāda* and *bindu*, and is adorned with the *vidārī* [mudrā]. 20.
She has a face like the sky, bears the smoke-bannered fire, and is an elephant; she is the fire of universal dissolution.
Her hair stands erect, she is mounted upon a corpse, and she is joined with a dot and the half-moon.
The seed-syllable of Ānandabhairavī, which brings supreme bliss to the mute: HSKHPHREṂ.

in the letter *ā* is Tāmasī, Kālavajrī (or Kālavajrī-jihvā), and Kālabhairavī.

Dharā, kṣmā, bhūḥ, sthirā, jyā, kūr, gotrā, bhūmī, rasā, and ilā—these are declared by the wise to be the names of the ten colors of the earth. (58)
Jalam, vāri, vanam, vāḥ, kam, pāthaḥ, toyam, rasaḥ, ambu, and hṛt—these ten names for water have been declared as its designations by the ancient sages. (59)
Vibhu, kha, svardyu, abhra, vyoman, śūnya, nabhas, and viyat;
haṃsa and ākāśa are the designations for the vowels [a and au], while māyā is so called because of its emission (visarga). 60.
This designation of phonemes has been proclaimed as taught in the Svatantra-tantra. || 61 ||
Thus ends the Lexicon of Colors as declared in the Rudrayāmala Tantra.
Now follows the description of the seed-syllables (bīja) as taught in the Bhūtaḍāmara Tantra.
Having extracted from the tantric scriptures for the sake of understanding the conventions of seed-syllables,
I shall state a few names of these seeds for the delight of the learned.
Seated upon blood, with a face like the sky, adorned by Dhūmrabhairavī, and joined with Nāda and Bindu—this is remembered as the first seed-syllable: Hrīṃ.
Māyā, Lajjā, Parā, Saṃvit, the three-guṇa Bhuvaneśvarī,
Hṛllekhā, Śambhuvanitā, Śakti, Devīśvarī, and Śivā.
Mahāmāyā and Pārvatī, who assumes forms through her various manifestations; the Supreme Goddess, the sustainer of the worlds, dwelling within the life-force. Hrīṃ.
The *māyā* (hrlīṃ) joined with fire (ra), Indra (la), and *māyā* (hrīṃ) is proclaimed as the *sthiramāyā*. Hlīṃ.
The syllable *śāgni* (Śrīṃ), together with the *śānti*, *bindu*, and *nāda*, is called the *lakṣmīpraṇava*. Śrī, Lakṣmī, Viṣṇuvanitā, Ramā, and Kṣīrasamudrajā are her names. Śrīṃ.
This is known as the seed-syllable of the bride (vadhū-bīja), consisting of sixteen consonants, joined with the fire (ra), the left eye (ī), and the bindu, and mounted upon the moon-seed (a).
A young bride, a woman with beautiful eyes, a woman with one eye, a female, and a loving woman—these are synonyms for *strī*.
The twelfth vowel, conjoined with *nāda* and *bindu*, is the *bhaga*;
the *yoni* is the seed-syllable of Sarasvatī; the lower part is the *vāgbhava*, which is speech. *Aiṃ*.
The syllable *ha*, enriched by the left ear (the vowel *u*) and adorned with the *nāda* and *bindu*, is called the *kūrca*, the wrathful, fierce pride, the long *hūṃ*. 4.
And the sound is "Dīrghakavaca," as well as "Tārāpraṇava": HŪṂ.
The syllable of Kāma situated in fire (Ra), adorned with Rati and the Bindu—this is declared to be the seed-syllable of Kālī; indeed, that very same thing is the seed-syllable of Rati. *Krīṃ*.
The syllable of desire (KĀM), situated on the earth (L) and adorned with the drop of delight (bindu),
is this seed-syllable of Guhyakālī, also known as the seed-syllable of Gopāla.
That is the seed-syllable of Kāma, the seed-syllable of Kāmeśī: *klīṃ*. Within Śakti is *sauḥ*, which is Parā; *sauḥ*.
The Śaiva Prāsāda is said to consist of the number of truths (4), the ends of the yugas (4), the sky (0), and the moon (1): HAUM.

The first [syllable] of *kalā* is the seed-syllable *Kledinī*: *klhrīṃ*. The syllable *kroṃ* is called the *aṅkuśa*. The letter *ā* endowed with the *bindu* is declared to be the *pāśa*, and the remainder is *śeṣa*: *āṃ*.
Sakalā Bhuvaneśānī is said to be the seed-syllable (bīja) of Kāmeśī: KLHRĪM.
*Namastu* is the heart; *namaḥ* [is the head]; *svāhā*, the pair of *dviṭha-ṣṭha*, and *ṭhaṭhaḥ* [are the crown].
16. The pair of moons is the head; the Mother of the Gods is Jvalanasundarī.
Svāhā; Parā; Devabhojya; the two Ṭhas; the pair of Candras;
Śruva; Havis; Vedamātā; Devāsya; Vahnisundarī; Svāhā.
The *śikhā* (crown lock) is *vaṣaṭ*, the center of the head; she is the mother of Śakra and the beloved of Hara. 20. *Kavaca* (armor) is *krodha* (wrath), the armor is *huṃ*;
that which is called wrath is *huṃ*, and it is the armor. At the beginning of the weapon-mantra, there is the one known as the enemy, *huṃ*. *Huṃ*.
The weapon-mantra for the pair of eyes is *vauṣaṭ*. *Vauṣaṭ*. *Phaṭ* is the weapon, the missile, the armament. *Phaṭ*. (p. 63) 1.
The third [seed-syllable] is *hsauḥ*, the seed of the *preta*. *hesauḥ*. *Haṃsaḥ* is the *ajapā* mantra. *Haṃsaḥ*.
The syllable *ga* accompanied by the *bindu* is the seed-syllable (*bīja*) of Vighnarāja, the seed-syllable of Gaṇeśa: *gaṃ*.
The seed-syllable of the Earth (Bhū-bīja), accompanied by the letter 'ma' with a dot (bindu) and situated in memory, is proclaimed as "glauṃ."
The seed-syllable of the Bimba is the letter *ṭha*, joined with fire (*ra*), the eye (*i*), and the moon (*u*): *ḍrīṃ*.
Then, the Kāmakalā is the left eye joined with the Bindu: Īṃ.
The half-mora is Kalā, Vāṇī, Nāda, Ardhendu, and Sadāśiva.
The fourth is unutterable, the supreme digit that is the mother of the universe; *gūṃ* is the resonance (*nāda*).
Now, the names of the seed-syllables (bīja) as stated in the Bhūtaḍāmara Tantra:
The *praṇava* is the poison-seed (*viṣabīja*); it is certainly known as *hālāhala*.
*Kāla* is to be known as *śrutimukha*, while *bahurūpin* is *nirañjana*. [This refers to] the *praṇava*.
Situated in blood, with the sky as its face, adorned by Dhūmra-Bhairavī, and joined with Nāda and Bindu—this is remembered as the primary seed-syllable: Hrīṃ.
Krodhīśa is mounted upon blood, adorned by Dhūmrabhairavī, joined with Nāda and Bindu, and is known as Pitṛbhūvāsinī. KṚĪṂ.
One should form Krodha, whose nature is Time (Kālātmaka), or the elemental Vāgbhava;
having taken it together with Nāda and Bindu, one obtains Ugrabhairavī.
This seed-syllable has been declared as that which sets pure intellect in motion. Aiṃ.
Krodhīśa, Balabhit, Dhūmrabhairavī, Nāda, and Bindu;
Trimūrti, Manmatha, Kāmarāja, and Tryailokyamohana: KLĪM.
Brahmā seated upon Indra’s throne is indeed Manmatha, the god of love, possessing six forms. Klīm.
Joined with Dhūmrabhairavī, the supreme seed-syllable of Kiṅkiṇī is "balibhojana" (the eater of offerings) situated in red, conjoined with Nāda and Bindu: DRĪṂ.
(Aligned with the *nāda* and *bindu*, residing in the blood, the consumer of offerings,
seated upon the throne of Kālarātri— this is the great mantra of the Lord of Arrows: *druṃ*.)*
Embracing Vidyārī in the secret place, the flesh-eater (Piśitāśana) is smeared with blood and joined with the *nāda* and *bindu*; he is to be known as *Drūṃ*.
The seed-syllable that brings about the end of the age, consisting of smoke-bannered fire with upward-pointing hair and the moon-bindus, was revealed by Bhairava: SPHEṂ.
Having taken up [the mantra] of Kapardin, whose body is drenched in blood;
joined with Dhūmrabhairavī, this is the crow (dhvāṅkṣa) possessing the sound (nāda) and the bindu: *Prīṃ*.
Taking up two skull-bowls adorned with Mahākāla, that pair is further described as being enriched by Caṇḍikā and captivating to the mind. *ṭhaṭhaṃ ṭhaḥṭhaḥ*.

That which stands upon blood, has the sky as its face, and is adorned with the dot (bindu), the crescent moon, and the half-moon, is proclaimed as Khadyota; it is conjoined with Grāsinī and Kālarātri. Hraṃ hruṃ.
The sky drenched in blood, adorned with the *nāda* and *bindu*, and further embellished by the *vidārī*, is the seed-syllable whose nature is that of Vaivasvata: *hrūṃ*.
She is named Kīrti, she has a mouth of time, and she is adorned by Mahākāla.
The Creator is the beginning of the sun and other luminaries, possessing five rays, and he is the one who effects creation, preservation, and destruction. Om.
Situated in the sky, the *kūrca* (the syllable *hrīṃ*) resides within the *nāda* and *jaṅghā*; it is adorned with the *bindu* and *nāda*.
Kāla, Mahākāla, and the seed-syllable of Wrath (*krodhabīja*) are stainless. *Hūṃ*.
Thus ends the exposition of the seed-syllables as taught in the Bhūtaḍāmara Tantra.
Now follows the exposition of the meaning of the mantras taught in the Varadā Tantra.
1. O Supreme Goddess, listen as I now explain the meaning of the mantra;
without it, O Śivā, success cannot be achieved even through millions of spiritual practices.
First, O Pārvatī, hear the meaning of the mantra which is the seed of grace:
the letter *ha* denotes Śiva, while the vowel *au* is Sadāśiva.
It is empty, yet for the purpose of removing suffering; therefore, one should worship Śiva with that [mantra]. HAUṂ.
O Goddess, the letter *ū* denotes Durgā and also signifies protection; Viśvamātā is the form of *nāda*, while the letter *k* in the sense of "doing" takes the form of the *bindu*.
Therefore, O Śivā, one should worship Durgā with that very same seed-syllable: *dūṃ*.
The letter *ka* is declared by Brahmā to signify Kālī; the letter *ī* signifies Mahāmāyā; the *nāda* signifies Viśvamātā; and the *bindu* signifies the remover of suffering.
With that very [mantra], one should worship Kālikā Devī for the pacification of suffering: KRĪṂ.
The letter *ha* is the designator of Śiva; the letter *ra* is said to be primordial nature (*prakṛti*).
The word *ī* signifies Mahāmāyā, and *nāda* is remembered as the progenitor of the universe.
One should worship with "duḥkhaharāthako binduḥ bhuvanāntena" and "hrīṃ."
The letter Śa signifies Mahālakṣmī; the letter Ra is said to signify wealth.
The letter I signifies satisfaction, while the supreme Nāda signifies the remover of suffering.
This is the seed-syllable (bīja) of the goddess Lakṣmī; with it, one should worship the goddess. Śrīṃ.
The syllable *ai* signifies Sarasvatī, and the bindu signifies the remover of suffering;
this is the seed-syllable (*bīja*) of Sarasvatī, and with it one should worship Vāṇī: *aiṃ*.
Who is designated as Kāmadeva, or is he called Kṛṣṇa?
The letter *la* signifies Indra, while *ī* denotes contentment; and *aṃ* bestows both happiness and suffering.
O Maheśvarī, out of affection for you, I have explained to you the meaning of the seed-syllable of desire: *klīṃ*.
Ha is said to be Śiva, O Goddess, while U is here called Bhairava.
The word Nāda signifies the supreme goal, while Bindu has the meaning of the remover of suffering.
Indeed, the seed-syllable of the armor has been taught to you here as "huṃ."

The letter *ga* has been told to you as having the meaning of Gaṇeśa; the nasal dot (*bindu*) signifies the remover of suffering. The seed-syllable *gaṃ* has thus been explained to you out of affection, O Maheśvarī. *Gaṃ*.
The letter *la* is considered by the wise to have the meaning of pervading Gaṇeśa and to signify splendor (*tejas*).
The nasal dot (*bindu*) signifies the remover of suffering; with that, one should worship Gaṇeśa. *Glauṃ*.
The syllable *kṣa* signifies Nṛsiṃha and Brahmā; the vowel *u* signifies the upper teeth. The nasal dot (*bindu*) signifies the remover of suffering. With that, one should worship Nṛsiṃha: *KṢRAUṂ*.
The first letter of the name of all things was declared as "Name" (nāman) by the Self-Existent One;
one should understand the meaning through that very [name], and one should contemplate what is implied by the meaning.
O Śivā, one should contemplate the meaning of the mantra according to the meaning of each respective case-ending;
this has been told to you in brief by means of the application of those respective syllables and so forth.
The letter *ta* is said to signify the crossing over of difficulties and the purpose of liberation;
the letter *ra* is stated here to signify enjoyment (*bhukti*), and the letter *ī* signifies Mahāmāyā.
The *nāda* is the mother of the universe, and the *bindu* signifies the remover of suffering.
O Maheśvarī, out of affection for you, the meaning of the seed-syllable of the bride (*badhū*) has been explained here as *strīṃ*. (p. 67) 1.
In a mantra where there are two *bindus*, one is for the purpose of removing suffering and the other is for bestowing happiness; O Goddess, having understood this, one should contemplate its meaning.
4. Where there are two *bindus* in the mantra, another [syllable] is considered to have the sense of "fulfillment" (*pūrṇa*).
O Goddess, *svāhā* is proclaimed to have the sense of "measure" (*mātrā*) or to be for the sake of the supreme goal (*parārtha*).

One should designate *vaṣaṭ* as the mother of Śakra, a speech intended for the beloved of Hari; *phaṭ* is for the sake of the gods, and one should point out *vinṛm* as the seed-syllable (*bīja*) in Hayagrīva.
The seed-syllable *yaṃ* is said to belong to Vāyu, while *laṃ* is proclaimed as belonging to Indra;
and in the case of multi-syllabic seed-mantras, one's own seed-syllable is that which corresponds to one's own name.
Having understood this, O Great Goddess, one should contemplate the meaning of the mantra;
where there is a single seed-syllable or two, one should conceive of them as having distinct meanings.
Or else, O Maheśānī, having understood the mantra for the purpose of repetition, one should indeed recite it with the intellect.
Thus, O Goddess, O Supreme Sovereign, the meaning of the mantra has been told to you.
Thus ends the exposition of the meaning of the mantras taught in the Varadātantra.
Now, the glossary of mudrās (Mudrānighaṇṭu) 1. [Regarding the etymological derivation of the word *mudrā*, the *Yāmala* states:]

Because she gladdens all the gods and dissolves the succession of sins, she is known as Mudrā; she is the means for accomplishing all desires and aims. I shall proclaim those [mudrās] which are hidden in all the tantras, and by the performance of which the deities of the mantras rejoice. (1)
And during the time of secret recitation, in meditation, and in rites performed for specific desires; 4. as well as in bathing, invocation, [the use of] the conch, consecration, and protection. 2.
Regarding the food offering and likewise the cooked rice revealed in their respective ritual manuals (kalpas),
the mudrās should be performed in their proper places, endowed with their individual characteristics.
The nine mudrās beginning with the invocation (āvāhana) are considered common [to all rites];
likewise, one should employ the six-limbed mudrās (ṣaḍaṅgamudrā) in all mantras. 4.
The wise have declared that Viṣṇu has nineteen mudrās:
the conch, the discus, the mace, the lotus, the flute, the śrīvatsa, and the kaustubha; || 5 ||
The forest-garland (vanamālā), the knowledge-seal (jñānamudrā), that which is called the bilva fruit, and the supreme seal known as Garuḍa—these grant satisfaction to Viṣṇu. 12–6.
Nārasiṃhī, Vārāhī, Hayagrīvī, and likewise Dhanuḥ; then Bāṇa-mudrā, Parśu, and the supreme Jagannohanikā.
The Kāmamudrā is proclaimed as the supreme; these are the ten mudrās of Śiva:
the Liṅga, the Yoni, the Trident, the Rosary, the Aṣṭa (Eight), the Bhīma (Terrible), and the Deer. || 8 ||
The khaṭvāṅga, the one called kapāla, and the ḍamaru grant satisfaction to Śiva;
for Sūrya there is only one, called padma; and these are the seven mudrās of Gaṇeśa. 4–9.
The mudrās known as the tooth, the noose, the goad, the obstacle-remover, the staff, the ball, and the citron should be understood as being employed in the worship of Vighna (Gaṇeśa). 10.
The noose, goad, boon-granting gesture, fear-dispelling gesture, sword, shield, bow, and arrow;
8. The mace-gesture, the ring-gesture, and the Durga-gesture are the mudrās that bring joy to Śakti. 11.
The Mudgara, the one called Pāśa-vajra, the tongue, and likewise Brāhmī—
these are declared to be the five mudrās in the recitation and worship of the Brahmā-astra.

In the worship of Lakṣmī’s mudrā, [one uses] Lakṣmī; in the worship of Vāg-vādinī, however, [there are] the rosary (akṣamālā), the lute (vīṇā), and the mudrās of the book for exposition (vyākhyā-pustaka). 12–13.
The mudrā called Saptajihvā should be known for the worship of Fire;
likewise, the Matsya-mudrā, the one named Kūrma, the Lelihā, and the one designated as Muṇḍa. (14)
Known as the Great Yoni (Mahāyoni), she bestows the abundance of all spiritual accomplishments (siddhis).
(16) In the worship of Śakti, [the mudrā] is Mahāyoni; in the case of Śyāmā and others, it is Muṇḍamudrikā. (15)
The mudrās known as Matsya, Kūrma, and Lelihā are considered common;
however, the five specific mudrās for the worship of Tārā are now described. (16)
Yoni, Bhūtinī, Bījākhyā, Daityadhūminī, and Lelihānā—these are declared to be the five mudrās that have been observed. 20–17.
Ten mudrās are fully described for the worship of Tripurā:
Saṃkṣobha (agitation), Drāvaṇa (melting), Ākarṣa (attracting), Vaśya (subjugating), Unmāda (intoxication), and Mahāṅkuśa (the great goad).
The ten [mudrās] known as Khecarī, Bīja, Yoni, and Trikhaṇḍā have been proclaimed.
The Kumbha-mudrā is used for consecration, and likewise the Padma-mudrā for the seat. 19.
Kālakarṇī should be employed for the rite of pacifying obstacles;
Gālinī should be employed for the rite of purifying water.
In the worship of Śrī Gopāla, one should display the flute; for Nṛhari, the Nārasiṃhikā;
and in the worship of Varāha, one should exhibit the form known as Vārāhā. (21)
In the worship of Hayagrīva, one should likewise display the Hayagrīvī mudrā;
in the worship of Rāma, the bow and arrow mudrās; and in the worship [of Śiva], the axe mudrā.
This [mudrā] of Paraśurāma is to be known as Jaganmohanā;
it is the Kāmamudrā used in the worship of Jaganmohana and in his adoration.
In the meditation on the one called Vāsudeva, the *kumbha-mudrā* is used for protection;
in all instances of petitioning, one should display the mudrā known as *prārthanā*.
Taking up what was not mentioned in the summary, their characteristics are now stated:
having formed the añjali with both hands, [one places the fingers] at the root-joints of the ring fingers. || 25 ||
One should place the two thumbs [within the palms]; this is known as the *āvāhanī* (invocation) mudrā.
If this same mudrā is turned face downwards, it is known as the *sthāpanī* (installation) mudrā.
From the joining of two fists with the thumbs raised, it is the *sannidhāpanī* [mudrā];
that same mudrā, when the thumbs are inserted inside, is considered the *saṃbodhinī*. (27)
With both hands open and palms facing each other, this is considered the *sammukhīkaraṇī* [mudrā]. 20.
The ritual placement (*nyāsa*) of the six limbs upon the body of the deity constitutes the *sakalīkṛti*. 28.
A fist formed with the left hand, with the index finger extended and pointing downward—
this is considered the *avaguṇṭhana* mudrā when it is rotated all around.
With the little fingers and ring fingers again joined face-to-face,
and likewise the index and middle fingers, this is declared to be the *dhenu-mudrā*. (30)
The best of practitioners should perform the rite of immortalization (amṛtīkaraṇa) with that [mudrā]. 4.
With the thumbs interlaced and the fingers of the hands extended, 31.
This great mudrā is joyous when perfected by the wise;
one should employ these mudrās in the rite of summoning the deity. (32)
The mudrās capable of being applied to the limbs are now described; their characteristics are stated as follows. || 33 ||
The fingers of the hand should be straight and without the thumb; this [gesture] is the mudrā for the heart and the head.
Indeed, the fist with the thumb tucked underneath is for the topknot (śikhā).
The fingers of both hands should be placed upon the armor. || 34 ||
The sound produced by the thumbs and index fingers raised from the two hands held in the *nārāca* fist,
resonating all around, is declared to be the *astra-mudrā*.
In this [mudrā], the index fingers and middle fingers are positioned at the eyes. || 35 ||
Where there are three eyes, it is called Anāmā;
thus the six-limbed mudrās have been described by those who know the ritual rules.
One should provide the missing limbs for a mantra that lacks them by means of its own [components].
Now, the characteristics of the Vaiṣṇava mudrās are described.
Having grasped the left thumb with the right fist, one should then turn the fist upward and extend the thumb. 38.
The fingers of the left hand are thus joined together, well-extended,
and touched by the right thumb; this is declared to be the *śaṅkha-mudrā*.
Having brought the two hands together facing each other, with the fingers slightly bent and pressed close, the thumbs joined within the palms, well-curved and well-stretched out. || 40 ||
The little finger and the thumb joined together—this is the mudrā known as the wheel (cakrasaṃjñikā).
Having placed the two hands facing each other with the fingers interlaced... 41.
Furthermore, when the two middle fingers are well-joined and properly extended,
this is declared to be the Gadā-mudrā (mace gesture) of Viṣṇu, which increases his satisfaction.
Having brought the two hands together facing each other,
with the fingers slightly bent and the thumbs joined at the palms— this is the mudrā known as Padma.
The thumb of the left hand is placed upon the lip;
there, the little finger is joined with the right thumb, while that [right] little finger is extended.
The index, middle, and ring fingers slightly bent and moved [together]—this shall be the flute mudrā, well-guarded and dear to Hari. (45)
One should join the middle and ring fingers of the two hands, which are touching one another, by binding them with the thumbs resting at the base of the little fingers. (46)
One should form the two index fingers; this mudrā is named Śrīvatsa.
The little finger of the right hand is joined to the back of the ring finger.
Having bound [the left hand] with the other little finger and likewise with the right index finger,
one should bind the left ring finger at the base of the right thumb.
Having joined the left thumb and middle finger together, with the other four fingers extended and wet, their tips touching one another—this is the mudrā known as Kaustubha. (49)
One should touch [the body] from the throat down to the feet using the index finger and the little finger of both hands; this mudrā, like a garland, is called the Vanamālikā. (50)
One should place the index finger and thumb joined together in a curved shape at the heart;
then one should place the lotus-like left hand upon the crown of the left knee.
This shall be the knowledge-seal (jñānamudrā), the beloved of Rāmacandra.
Having raised the left thumb and bound its tip with the thumb of the other hand, and having firmly bound those fingers of the left hand with the fingers [of the right],
the one of pure intellect should place it against the heart while reciting the seed-syllable of Māra.
This ring, known as Vilva, has been clearly described here; it must be kept secret by those who know the ritual procedure.
Having turned the two hands away from each other and joined the two little fingers,
one should likewise join the two index fingers and the two thumbs together.
One should move the two middle and ring fingers like two wings;
this is the Garuḍa-mudrā, which increases the satisfaction of Viṣṇu.
Placing his hands between his knees, with his chin and lips held level,
his hands remained fixed upon the ground, trembling again and again.
Having turned the face back and flicking the tongue, this shall be the Nārasiṃhī mudrā, which increases his delight. || 57 ||
Then, having grasped the two little fingers with the two thumbs of both hands, while all the other fingers are turned downward— this is known as the mudrā of Nṛhari.
The wise one should place the left hand palm-upward over the right;
this is declared to be the mudrā known as Vārāhī. 59.
The right hand facing upward and the left hand facing downward,
with the tips of the fingers joined together, is the mudrā known as Vārāhī.

Having placed the fingers of the right hand face-down upon the palm of the left hand, and having fixed the middle and ring fingers, one should bend them downward below the mouth, raising the middle finger [in some versions it says "having raised the middle finger from among those"]. 61.
The mudrā dear to Hayagrīva imitates his form: one should join the tips of the middle fingers of the left hand with the tips of the index fingers. 62.
One should press the ring finger and the little finger with its thumb and touch them to the left shoulder; this is declared to be the bow mudrā (dhanurmudrā).
The arrow-mudrā is formed by the right fist with the index finger extended. [Regarding the characteristics of another type of arrow-mudrā, it is said in the Jñānārṇava]:
"O Dear One, make the hand like a bow held in the hand;
